items.readable_text:
Content:
How can we calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{\int} \left(3\sin^2 x + 3\cos^2 x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x?]

Content:
We can compute integrals like this using the Pythagorean trigonometric identity,
[MATH: \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x=1.]

Content:
So, we evaluate our integral as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \eqalign{
\int \left(3\sin^2 x+ 3\cos^2 x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x &= \int 3(\underbrace{\sin^2 x +\cos^2 x }_1 )\, \textrm{d}x\
&=\int 3(1) \, \textrm{d}x\
&=\int 3 \, \textrm{d}x\
&=3x+C
}]

Content:
Let's look at some more examples.

We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

[MATH: \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.]

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(1 − \sin^{2} x)dx|= ∫(1)/(\cos^{2} x)dx; = ∫((1)/(\cos x))^{2}dx; = ∫\sec^{2} xdx; = \tan x + C.]

key_prerequisites.name: Alternate Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity

sections.normalized_html:
First, we select the identity that contains a [MATH: \tan^2{x}] term. So we can use the identity [MATH: 1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.] Rearranging the above identity gives [MATH: \tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.]

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\ &=\tan x -x+C. }]

In this case, we have to use the identity [MATH: 1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.] Rearranging this gives

Substituting this into our integral gives

items.title: Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities

sections.normalized_html:
From the identity [MATH: 1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta] with [MATH: \theta = 3x,] we get

[MATH: \eqalign{ 1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\ \tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1. }]

Substituting the above into our integral gives

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\ &= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\ &= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\ &= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C. }]

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{\int} 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d} x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the identity [MATH: 1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta] with [MATH: \theta = 3x,] we get

[MATH: \eqalign{
1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}]

Substituting the above into our integral gives

[MATH: \eqalign{
\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
&= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
&= \dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
}]

Item 12 — Example: Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle{\int} 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d} x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the identity [MATH: 1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta] with [MATH: \theta = 3x,] we get

[MATH: \eqalign{
1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}]

Substituting the above into our integral gives

[MATH: \eqalign{
\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
&= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
&= \dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
}]
